Eskom after Lockdown

By: Joy Summers | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
What happens when most of us return to work and Eskom has to keep the lights on again? Will South Africans battered by Covid19 and lockdown have to endure the threat of the v

Unique Selling Point:
A one on one interview with the New CEO Andre de Ruyter and exclusive information on Medupi and Kusile design flaws

Summary:
Summary
Load shedding, increased electricity prices, a broken fleet of power stations and fatal design flaws on Medupi and Kusile, and a debt of R450 billion rand that hangs over the country like the sword of Damocles. These are all challenges for the new CEO.


Further information:
So what has been happening at Eskom during lockdown. We dive deep into the flaws of Medupi and Kusile and why they happened, who pays for them and what Eskom are doing to fix the problem. We challenge de Ruyter on the transparency and accountability at Eskom. We explore why Eskom is breaking world bank covenants they signed and refusing to clean up their air pollution and we ask why South Africans should pay more for electricity when not a single Eskom executive has had to account for their malfeasance and Eskom is still burning through millions of litres of diesel on a daily basis.

Further information will encompass the two previous proposals and the contents of the recent frying session

FINAL SCRIPT ESKOM AFTER LOCKDOWN TX SUNDAY 31st MAY 2020

Commentary One
December 2019. Stage 6 load-shedding. Citizens fumed- Again! The president blamed power station sabotage, and the cabinet called for the new Eskom CEO to start earlier.

So, on Christmas day Andre De Ruyter took the helm at the failing power utility.

Masa
You have taken up what's been described as the worst job in the world. And critics have said that you can't possibly succeed, especially considering meddling ministers who think they know better?
Andre
I have not experienced that. We consult, but by and large I think the narrative of the minister micromanaging what Eskom does, is a gross exaggeration.

Commentary Two
De Ruyter has inherited a wasteland- a fleet of broken power stations driven into the ground, a debt of R450 billion rand that puts the entire country at risk, design flaws on Medupi and Kusile, and an organisation still reeling from state capture

Andre
We do have a mountain to climb, but it can be done. If I thought that it was an impossible assignment, I would definitely not have taken the job.

Commentary Three
At the recent state of the system briefing, there is a serious tone, and it’s clear that de Ruyter is putting pressure on team Eskom to perform.

Andre: I've been very fortunate to be supported by very capable and able team and I think that's something that the popular narrative about Eskom gets completely wrong.

Commentary Four
In March, Eskom warned parliament that Stage 8 load shedding would be a regular event if critical maintenance was not done. But lockdown has given them a buffer to reduce load shedding from a likely 30 days in winter down to 3, by adding 2000 MW to the grid

Andre:
Now to put that into perspective that's about a medium sized power station that we've added to the system that we think we can now bank on

Commentary Five
But the real maintenance work will only begin in July. And there is lots to be done. Engineer and founder chairman of the energy intensive user’s group, Mike Rossouw, was appointed by Eskom in 2014 to determine the state of all of Eskom’s power stations. It took seven months and he found 4700 major pieces of equipment that needed to be repaired, replaced or refurbished. But his report never saw the light of day, and he says then CEO Brian Molefe did not renew his contract

MIKE ROSSOUW
And between him and Matshela Koko, they then proceeded to talk up the whole Eskom performance and their own performance which was actually not true at all.

Commentary six
He also says Molefe and Koko cooked the books on maintenance

MIKE ROSSOUW
They absolutely did. And the way they did it simply, is the unplanned capacity losses, which basically means that the amount of breakdowns are clearly defined in Eskom own books, and what is a breakdown and what is planned work. And they changed those definitions to make breakdowns look like planned work, and that made their performance look good on paper, but it was in fact not the case.

Masa: We also hearing some strong allegations that Matshela Koko and Brian Molefe cooked the books when it comes to planned and planned maintenance.
Andre:
We have looked into this, because whenever you defer maintenance you borrow from the future. Claims are made that the lights were kept on but eventually the neglect becomes apparent and then you find yourself in a position where we have to do this reliability maintenance to catch up with the backlog.
Masa:
So there could be some truth to these allegations?
Andre:
I think that's something to be investigated, yes

Commentary Seven
We put those allegations to both Molefe and Koko. Molefe responded

Brian Molefe
I think it’s preposterous. Having said that- the electricity availability factor does not lie -
so even if you wiggle or change the definition of planned or unplanned it doesn’t change the EAF. When I was there, we increased the EAF from around 63% to 83% so we were doing maintenance and we increased our planned maintenance and we caught up with the back log of planned maintenance. We didn’t do what is alleged it really gets me hot under the collar, and to prove that we did not have load-shedding

Commentary Eight
Matshela Koko also denies the allegations. He says an independent audit of EAF and planned maintenance found that these key performance indicators were in all material respects fairly stated. He adds that he is pleased that under his and Brian Molefe’s leadership, the Eskom guardians met the country’s electricity demand without fail. He says that today, Eskom cannot meet the country’s electricity demand of 32 000MW without using diesel, and forcing the energy intensive user’s group to reduce their electricity by 10%.
He has posted the full version of his response on his twitter page

Commentary nine
But maintenance is only one of De Ruyter’s many challenges

LINK
About a year ago Eskom began to speak about design flaws on Medupi and Kusile. But these aren’t just minor flaws, they are massive engineering faults and if they are not fixed these two power stations will never ever work properly

Commentary ten
In February Eskom told parliament that all 12 of the boilers – 6 at Medupi and 6 at Kusile
would need to be raised by 12.5 metres. It turns out they had been designed too short. These are Kusile’s boilers during construction.

MIKE
I think first of all in terms of size think of the Carlton Centre, that's the kind of size that you're thinking of for a boiler.

Commentary eleven
Generating electricity begins by blowing pulverised coal as fine as talcum powder into the boilers and lighting it

MIKE
The boiler consists of a vast open area at the bottom where they create a fire ball. It's virtually like a sun, a very hot sun in the heart of the boiler. This heat rises and heats the pipes above the boiler which then creates steam. The steam is then used to drive the turbines

Commentary twelve
The dust and gasses then cool and are removed in pipes and captured in large material filter bags – but the shorter boiler designed and built by Hitachi now Mitsubishi, means the system overheats, and burns these huge filter bags and the downstream system

MIKE
And that was the situation that Eskom was stuck with that they were exhausting too hot gases and the consistency of the materials within those gases was such that the bags couldn't deal with it. Which basically means they destroyed the filter bags and the off-gas system takes enormous stresses which it's not designed to do.

Commentary Thirteen
Eskom says they have now found a work- around and will be able to get the power stations to full capacity, without raising the roof of each boiler. Their first experiment at Medupi Unit three was completed in 75 days a cost of R300 million rand.



Andre de Ruyter
And they were quite substantial defects, that really prevented us from running those units flat out. After implementing these design changes on Unit 3, within a matter of days it was able to for the first time ever reach its design capacity.

Commentary fourteen
Energy analyst Chris Yelland, said he would eat his hat if they completed the work on time

Masa
Chris you said that if Eskom was able to fix one boiler in 70 days you would eat your hat
They have done so in 75 days, so I have brought you your hat and some tomato sauce
Chris
It’s a little too early for that. Eskom made it very clear they haven’t proven they can sustain that/ it’s not about making a generator available for half an hour its making it available for a year can it perform at full output continuously for a year

Commentary fifteen
It was this same Hitachi boiler contract that was found to violate the foreign corrupt practices act. In 2015 Hitachi was fined 19 million US dollars by the United States Securities and Exchange Commission for making improper payments to then ANC company, Chancellor house.

Massa: Why is Eskom paying part of this cost when it was Hitachi, now Mitsubishi who did these designs in the first place?
Andre:
I think it's very important that we are pragmatic. The last thing that we wanted to do was to put the country at risk of load shedding while we squabble about who's going to pay for it.
Masa:
One of the experts we consulted with said had these designs been done properly from the get- go, we wouldn't have seen the levels of load shedding that we have seen?
Andre:
That that's absolutely spot on, decisions were made that were inadequately tested and motivated by facts. And we can complain about it but that's what happened

Commentary sixteen
These two power stations have also become the focus of investigations by the Special Investigating unit, who’s trying to recover misappropriated funds

LINK
So far 11 contracting companies have been identified and R139 billion that was funneled out of Eskom

Andre:
We are however doing everything we can to recover the money that's due to us, but it is a big process. It is it is clearing out the Aegean stables.


MASA
As recently as August last year, the former CEO said that there was still corruption at every single level in Eskom. On a scale of one to 10 how would you rate the clean up?
ANDRE
I think we are probably between three and a four in terms of the progress that we still need to make. We have conducted lifestyle audits on 383 senior Eskom employees as well as 272 spouses. Of this pool some 34 were referred for further investigation. So that gives you a size indication of what the challenge is

Commentary seventeen
And then there is also the R450 billion debt. Eskom is in a death spiral and can’t meet its debt obligations
Masa
Are we going to pay more for electricity?
Andre
Yes, you are going to pay more for electricity

Commentary eighteen
30 percent more according to Chris Yelland

Chris:
It would be extremely damaging to the economy, it would also be extremely damaging to Eskom. It may not have the the result they think because it may force people to look for other alternatives other than Eskom electricity

Commentary nineteen
So De Ruyter must also find a way to cut costs

Andre:
We are really scrutinizing every rand that we spend, but I have to say when I when I got to Eskom there was not sufficient focus in my view on ensuring that we spend our money as wisely as we can.

Commentary Twenty
Now De Ruyter is exploring the idea of rehabilitation of areas around the power stations and introducing clean energy using the existing infrastructure. That could unlock cheaper green energy finance and reduce debt payments. But not everyone is happy with Eskom’s new direction

Massa:
Our information is that the fightback campaign is beginning to hamper the investigation of the SIU and Eskom. Are you experiencing any resistance?
Andre:
I think Churchill said something along the lines of the dogs will bark but the train still steams forth. And I think that's the attitude that we've that we've got to have. Eskom is a is a is an enterprise of national importance. But the people who are resisting change because it closes the taps of opportunity. Well we don't have time and space for that.

THE END 12 01


PROMO ONE
With winter fast approaching and a perpetually unreliable power utility, will the new CEO Andre de Ruyter, really be able to turn the tables around

PROMO TWO
Load shedding, a fleet of broken power stations, design faults on Medupi and Kusile, Eskom CEO Andre De Ruyter says it’s a mountain to climb but it can be done

PROMO THREE
The state capture at Eskom and its enormous debt has put South Africa at risk. We sit down with CEO Andre De Ruyter to evaluate Eskom’s clean- up operation

Commentary Twenty Now De Ruyter is exploring the idea of rehabilitation of areas around the power stations and introducing clean energy using the existing infrastructure. That could unlock cheaper green energy finance and reduce debt payments. But not everyone is happy with Eskom’s new direction Massa: Our information is that the fightback campaign is beginning to hamper the investigation of the SIU and Eskom. Are you experiencing any resistance? Andre: I think Churchill said something along the lines of the dogs will bark but the train still steams forth. And I think that's the attitude that we've that we've got to have. Eskom is a is a is an enterprise of national importance. But the people who are resisting change because it closes the taps of opportunity. Well we don't have time and space for that.
